# Alignment files: SAM, BAM and CRAM {#sec-alignment-files}

An aligner takes each read and writes down **where in the genome it fits and
how**. The result is a **SAM** file (Sequence Alignment/Map), or its
compressed form, **BAM**. It's the biggest and richest file the pipeline
makes, and worth learning to read.

## SAM, BAM and CRAM

| | SAM | BAM | CRAM |
|---|---|---|---|
| Kind | Plain text | Binary, bgzip-compressed | Binary, compressed against the reference |
| Size | Huge | ~3–4× smaller than SAM | Smaller again |
| Read it with | `less` | `samtools view` | `samtools view` + the reference FASTA |
| In bagPipes | never written to disk | `output/align/*.bam` | not used |

The SAM text only ever exists inside the pipe in the `align` rule
(`hisat2 ... | samtools view -u | samtools sort ...`).

## The header

A BAM starts with header lines that begin with `@`:

```bash
samtools view -H output/align/IMGL_iMGL_WT_Ab_24h_1_1_sorted.bam | head
```

```
@HD  VN:1.0  SO:coordinate                         <- format version; sorted by coordinate
@SQ  SN:chr1  LN:248956422                         <- one line per chromosome: name, length
@SQ  SN:chr2  LN:242193529
...
@PG  ID:hisat2  PN:hisat2  VN:2.2.1  CL:"hisat2 -q -x ... -1 ... -2 ..."   <- programs that touched the file
@PG  ID:samtools ...
```

The `@PG` lines are a record of what was done to the file. Useful when
someone sends you a BAM and you want to know how it was made.

## The alignment lines: 11 columns

```bash
samtools view output/align/IMGL_iMGL_WT_Ab_24h_1_1_sorted.bam | head -2
```

```
A00123:456:HXXXXDSX2:1:1101:10004:1000  163  chr7  5527760  60  45M1102N55M  =  5528950  1290  TTGCAGG...  FFFF...  AS:i:0  NM:i:0  NH:i:1  XS:A:+
A00123:456:HXXXXDSX2:1:1101:10004:1000  83   chr7  5528950  60  100M         =  5527760  -1290 GCCCAGC...  FFFF...  AS:i:0  NM:i:0  NH:i:1
```

(Example lines.) Both mates of the pair appear, each on its own line.

| # | Column | Example | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | QNAME | `A00123:...:1000` | Read name, from the FASTQ header (same for both mates) |
| 2 | FLAG | `163` | A number encoding yes/no facts about the read (below) |
| 3 | RNAME | `chr7` | Chromosome it aligned to (`*` if unmapped) |
| 4 | POS | `5527760` | Leftmost aligned base, **1-based** |
| 5 | MAPQ | `60` | Mapping quality: how sure the aligner is this is the right place |
| 6 | CIGAR | `45M1102N55M` | How the read lines up with the genome (below) |
| 7 | RNEXT | `=` | Chromosome of the mate (`=` means the same) |
| 8 | PNEXT | `5528950` | Position of the mate |
| 9 | TLEN | `1290` | Distance spanned by the pair on the genome (includes introns) |
| 10 | SEQ | `TTGCAGG...` | The read's bases, **as they align to the + strand** |
| 11 | QUAL | `FFFF...` | Its quality string (same encoding as FASTQ) |
| 12+ | tags | `NH:i:1` | Optional extra fields, `TAG:TYPE:VALUE` |

::: {.callout-note}
## SEQ may be reverse-complemented

If a read aligned to the − strand, the SAM file stores its
**reverse complement**, so SEQ always reads left to right along the
reference. That is why SEQ in a BAM doesn't always match the FASTQ.
:::

### FLAG

The flag is the sum of these bits:

| Bit | Value | Meaning when set |
|---|---|---|
| 0x1 | 1 | Read is paired |
| 0x2 | 2 | Both mates aligned as a proper pair |
| 0x4 | 4 | This read is unmapped |
| 0x8 | 8 | Its mate is unmapped |
| 0x10 | 16 | This read aligned to the **reverse** strand |
| 0x20 | 32 | Its mate aligned to the reverse strand |
| 0x40 | 64 | This is **read 1** |
| 0x80 | 128 | This is **read 2** |
| 0x100 | 256 | **Secondary** alignment (another possible location of a multi-mapper) |
| 0x200 | 512 | Failed quality checks |
| 0x400 | 1024 | PCR or optical duplicate (only if a tool marked it) |
| 0x800 | 2048 | Supplementary alignment (chimeric/split read) |

So `163` = 128 + 32 + 2 + 1: read 2, mate on reverse strand, proper pair, paired.
And `83` = 64 + 16 + 2 + 1: read 1, on the reverse strand, proper pair, paired.
In a properly paired library you'll mostly see **99/147** and **83/163**.

Don't do this sum in your head: use `samtools flags 163` or
[Picard's flag explainer](https://broadinstitute.github.io/picard/explain-flags.html).

### CIGAR

The CIGAR string is a list of *length + operation*:

| Op | Meaning | Uses up read bases? | Uses up genome bases? |
|---|---|---|---|
| `M` | Aligned (match **or** mismatch) | yes | yes |
| `I` | Insertion in the read | yes | no |
| `D` | Deletion from the read | no | yes |
| `N` | **Skipped region: an intron** | no | yes |
| `S` | Soft clip: bases in the read but not aligned | yes | no |
| `H` | Hard clip: bases removed from SEQ | no | no |

`45M1102N55M` means 45 bases align, the next 1,102 bp of genome are skipped
(an intron), and the last 55 bases align in the next exon. **`N` is the
fingerprint of RNA-seq.** Only a splice-aware aligner writes it
([Tools](tools-landscape.qmd)).

### MAPQ

MAPQ = −10 log~10~ P(wrong location), but each aligner computes it in its
own way. For **HISAT2**, in practice:

| MAPQ | Meaning |
|---|---|
| 60 | Unique: one best location |
| 1 | Aligns equally well to 2 or more places |
| 0 | Aligns to many places |

### Tags you'll see from HISAT2

| Tag | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `NH:i:n` | Number of places this read aligned (1 = unique) |
| `AS:i:n` | Alignment score (0 is perfect; more negative is worse) |
| `NM:i:n` | Number of mismatches + indels vs the reference |
| `XS:A:+/-` | For spliced reads, the strand the intron motif implies (GT-AG on + or −) |
| `MD:Z:...` | Where the mismatches are |

## Sorted and indexed

HISAT2 writes reads in the order it reads them. `samtools sort` reorders
them by **chromosome and position** (`SO:coordinate` in the header), and
`samtools index` writes a `.bai` file next to the BAM. The index is a table
of contents: "chr7:5,500,000 starts at byte X". With it, IGV or `samtools
view` can jump straight to a region instead of reading the whole file.

**Keep the `.bai` next to its `.bam`, with the same name plus `.bai`.**

## samtools: the tool for BAM files

```bash
module load samtools/1.22
B=output/align/IMGL_iMGL_WT_Ab_24h_1_1_sorted.bam

samtools view -H $B                     # header only
samtools view $B | head                 # first alignments, as text
samtools view $B chr7:5527000-5531000 | wc -l   # alignments in a region (needs .bai)
samtools view -c $B                     # count alignment lines
samtools view -c -F 260 $B              # count primary mapped reads (exclude unmapped 4 + secondary 256)
samtools view -c -q 10 $B               # alignments with MAPQ >= 10
samtools view -f 2 -b $B > proper.bam   # keep only proper pairs (-f = must have flag)

samtools flagstat $B                    # summary (bagPipes saves this as _stats.txt)
samtools idxstats $B                    # reads per chromosome (chrM share is a QC signal!)
samtools stats $B | grep ^SN            # detailed summary numbers
samtools sort -n $B -o byname.bam       # sort by read name (some tools want this)
samtools merge merged.bam a.bam b.bam   # combine BAMs (the mergeAlign rule)
```

`-f` keeps reads that **have** the flag bits; `-F` keeps reads that **don't**.

### Reading `samtools flagstat`

bagPipes saves this for every sample as `align/{sample}_stats.txt`:

```
203512 + 0 in total (QC-passed reads + QC-failed reads)
200000 + 0 primary
3512 + 0 secondary
0 + 0 supplementary
0 + 0 duplicates
197612 + 0 mapped (97.10% : N/A)
194100 + 0 primary mapped (97.05% : N/A)
200000 + 0 paired in sequencing
100000 + 0 read1
100000 + 0 read2
188400 + 0 properly paired (94.20% : N/A)
...
```

(Example numbers.) Look at **primary mapped %** (how many reads found a
home) and **properly paired %**. "Total" can be more than the number of reads,
because secondary alignments are counted too.

## Looking at BAMs in IGV

1. Download `{sample}_sorted.bam` **and** `{sample}_sorted.bam.bai` to the
   same folder (or open them from a mounted drive).
2. In IGV, choose the same genome (**hg38**), then *File → Load from File*.
3. Type a gene name (e.g. `ACTB`) in the location box.

What you'll see: grey bars are reads; thin lines joining them are **introns
spliced across** (`N` in the CIGAR); coloured letters are mismatches; a
coverage histogram on top. Right-click → *Group alignments by → first-of-pair
strand* to see strandedness.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Check your understanding

1. A read has FLAG `99`. Decode it.
2. What does the CIGAR `3S97M` mean?
3. Why does `samtools view $B chr1:1000-2000` fail without a `.bai` file?
4. `idxstats` shows 30 % of reads on `chrM`. What might that mean?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple"}
## Answers

1. 64 + 32 + 2 + 1: read 1, mate on the reverse strand, proper pair, paired.
   (This read is on the forward strand.)
2. The first 3 bases are soft-clipped (present in the read but not aligned,
   often leftover adapter or a mismatch at the end), then 97 bases align.
3. Without the index samtools can't jump to a region; it would have to
   scan the whole file, and it refuses to.
4. A lot of mitochondrial RNA. That's common in some cell types, but very high
   values can indicate stressed or dying cells, or a cytoplasm-heavy prep.
:::
:::
